newsitem.title: INDIA: New India premier says wants trade, not blocs.
newsitem.headline: New India premier says wants trade, not blocs.

text.p: India's new prime minister Inder Kumar Gujral on Monday turned down an idea for an economic triangle with Russia and China, saying he favoured close economic ties with traditional friends without the formation of economic blocs.
"We don't want to build any blocs, we want to build friendships," he said at his first public meeting after assuming the post of Prime Minister earlier in the day.

Gujral, who was addressing a business conference organised by the Confederation of Indian Industry (CII), was asked if India would be interested in forming a trilateral economic bloc with Russia and China.
The former Soviet Union was a close ally of India during the Cold War, and New Delhi has sustained efforts to maintain warm relations with Moscow.
India has also recently worked towards closer ties with China, with whom it fought a brief border war in 1962.
"We have fortunately very good relations with Russia and China but we do not want to build any blocs," Gujral said.

Gujral, who was foreign minister in Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's cabinet ousted earlier this month, said India was a big country, an old, peace-loving civilization which would not confine itself to any blocs.

Gujral, who played a key role in reviving high-level talks after a three-year gap with arch-rival Pakistan and signing a landmark water treaty with Bangladesh, said India will try its best to create good neighbourly relations in Asia.
"I am hopeful that we will succeed in our endeavour to improve our relations with neighbours, both in trade and otherwise," Gujral said.

Gujral was sworn in as India's 12th prime minister on Monday as the leader of the 15-party centre-left United Front, ending three weeks of political uncertainty linked to uneasy relations with its make-or-break ally, the Congress party.

Gujral replaced Deve Gowda, who stepped down as the coalition's parliamentary leader under an agreement to please the Congress party after his government was defeated in a confidence vote on April 11.
